common_name: Carolina Ruby Sweet Potato (Early Deep-Red-Skin Orange Sweet Potato)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F; ridge rows to keep the developing roots loose and well-drained.

directions: Carolina Ruby was bred at North Carolina State University and released in the late 1990s as an earlier-maturing companion to Beauregard, with striking deep red-purple skin and moist orange flesh. It bulks up quickly and can be dug a couple of weeks ahead of most other orange sweet potatoes, which is a real advantage for beating fall's first frost in a home garden. Vines are thin and trailing rather than bushy, so give them room to ramble or trellis them along a fence. Roots can develop pronounced lenticels if soil stays wet close to harvest, so time digging for a dry stretch and avoid heavy irrigation in the final weeks.
sources: NC State University Plant Breeding Consortium

common_name: Carolina Bunch Sweet Potato (Compact Bush-Type for Small Gardens)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is reliably warm; the short, compact vines make this a good candidate for raised beds or large containers.

directions: Carolina Bunch was developed at North Carolina State University specifically for small-space growers, with a tight, semi-bush habit that stays under 3 feet of spread instead of sprawling 6-8 feet like standard vining sweet potatoes. Despite the compact vines, it is a solid producer of light copper-skinned, dark orange-fleshed roots that store and bake well. Because the plants don't sprawl and cover ground the way most sweet potatoes do, keep the bed mulched to suppress weeds and maintain even soil moisture. This is a practical choice for raised beds or anywhere a gardener wants sweet potatoes without letting vines take over the whole plot.
sources: NC State University Plant Breeding Consortium

common_name: Sumor Sweet Potato (Dry White-Fleshed Baking Type)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost in warm soil; Sumor needs a full, long warm season to size up its roots properly.

directions: Sumor stands apart from most named sweet potato cultivars by being dry and mild rather than sweet and moist, with tan-to-yellow skin and firm white to pale yellow flesh that holds its shape when cooked. It behaves in the kitchen more like a russet potato than a typical Southern sweet potato, making it a useful choice for cooks who want a starchy, low-sugar substitute for regular potatoes in a Gulf Coast garden too hot for real potatoes in summer. The vines are vigorous and the roots show good field resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode, both common headaches in Southern sweet potato beds. Because it is slower to mature than orange types, get slips in the ground as early as the last frost date allows.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Regal Sweet Potato (Disease-Resistant Southern Baking Type)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed; Regal matures quickly and does well even in a shorter warm season.

directions: Regal was jointly developed by the USDA and the South Carolina and Texas agricultural experiment stations as a reliable, disease-resistant sweet potato for Southern home gardens and market growers. Its light orange skin and flesh give a classic sweet, moist baked texture, and broad resistance to common soil diseases and insect pests makes it more forgiving than many older heirlooms in beds that have grown sweet potatoes before. It matures a bit faster than many standard orange cultivars, which is useful insurance in a Gulf Coast garden where an early tropical storm can end the season abruptly. Grow it the same way as Beauregard or Centennial, in loose, well-drained, ridged soil in full sun.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Diane Sweet Potato (Heavy-Yielding Louisiana Copper-Skin Type)

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost in warm, well-drained ridged soil; give Diane a full season since it is a heavier yielder than many faster-maturing cultivars.

directions: Diane was released by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station as a high-yielding sweet potato with smooth copper skin and deep orange flesh, developed to out-produce older Louisiana standards of its era. It shows useful tolerance to soil pox and resistance to white grubs, though like many older cultivars it is susceptible to root-knot nematode, so rotate beds or choose a nematode-resistant companion cultivar if that pest is a known problem in the garden. The vigorous vines and heavy root set reward rich, deeply worked soil and consistent moisture during the bulking stage in mid-to-late summer. Its dependable heavy yield made it a longtime favorite among Gulf Coast home growers before newer LSU releases like Beauregard and Evangeline became more widely available.
